title: Phosphatic limestone and horse country
summary: Inner Bluegrass soils rest on phosphatic Lexington and Cynthiana limestones, with high calcium and phosphorus. University of Kentucky soil tests still show that edge over the…
bodyMarkdown:
Kentucky's horse country starts underground. The Inner Bluegrass around Lexington rests on very old rock: the [Bluegrass region](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bluegrass_region) sits on the Cincinnati Arch, a broad fold that brings Ordovician limestones about 450 million years old close to the surface.

Some of those limestones are special. The Lexington and Cynthiana limestones are phosphatic, rich in phosphorus as well as calcium. As they weather, they make soils with more of both than most farmland in the state.

That shows up in the lab. University of Kentucky soil tests still find the Bluegrass ahead of the rest of Kentucky. In one late twentieth-century series, about two-thirds of Bluegrass samples tested high for phosphorus.

Phosphorus and calcium matter for grass, and grass matters for horses. The same ground grows thick pastures, including the bluegrass that gave the region its name. Before commercial fertilizer, a farmer could not easily add what the soil lacked. Land that was rich to begin with had a real edge, year after year.

Timing mattered too. From about 1780 to 1820, after the Revolution, families from Virginia and the Carolinas pushed west into the Bluegrass. Many of them came from horse-raising country and brought their breeding stock and their love of racing with them. They arrived just as a growing, industrial America needed more horsepower for farms, roads, and towns.

By 1826 Lexington horsemen had organized the [Kentucky Association race course](/stories/kentucky-association-1826-lexington-race-course/). The Thoroughbred farms that followed made the region the center of Kentucky's horse industry.

A long-told story says Bluegrass horses grow strong bones because the water and grass carry limestone. UK equine soil scientist Joshua McGrath argues the real story is not a magic-bone myth alone. It is [geology and settlement timing together](https://equine.mgcafe.uky.edu/content/how-soil-fertility-and-history-combined-make-kentucky%E2%80%99s-inner-bluegrass-region-%E2%80%9Chorse): high soil phosphorus supporting strong forage yields, and the right people arriving at the right moment.

## Kentucky today

The best place to see the result is the farm country of Fayette County. Pastures with plank and stone fences line the country roads around Lexington. The Kentucky Horse Park and Keeneland Race Course both welcome visitors, and many working Thoroughbred farms offer scheduled tours of their barns and paddocks.
Source: [University of Kentucky Equine: How soil fertility and history combined make Kentucky’s Inner Bluegrass region “Horse Capital of the World”](https://equine.mgcafe.uky.edu/content/how-soil-fertility-and-history-combined-make-kentucky%E2%80%99s-inner-bluegrass-region-%E2%80%9Chorse)
